A correct MatchDescendants/FunctionMatcher approach that returns (names, dynamic). Placeholders() hands out the internal slice without cloning, and the docs are not updated, but the unit and behavioral tests (including an upstream body check) are solid.

Clean use of ast.MatchDescendants and a separate dynamic flag, with good classifier and end-to-end tests; minor nits are that Placeholders() returns its internal slice uncloned and the field doc is left stale.

The design is clean and correct: a shared socket with a master file and a Close that runs under the lock and skips abstract sockets, and it covers newest-first closes. Moving count into a socket struct broke the internal API, and the package suite failed.
Logic is close to the reference plus a shared master file, but moving count into a separate socket struct breaks the hidden tests' internal field access, so 0/7 pass.

This is a thorough fix that even avoids the O_NONBLOCK flip from File().Fd() via a custom dup. It is very invasive, though: a pointer deleteListener, reordered pool logic, a listeners.go refactor and a GOOS-less abstract check. It also leaks the master file in one release path, and the package suite fails.

Thoughtful, including a raw-dup helper that avoids File() flipping the socket to blocking, but it refactors heavily (pointer delete wrappers, new state type, abstract helper moved into listeners.go without a GOOS check) and fails all hidden tests.

The refcounted shared-state rewrite is functionally sound, with tests that also cover the permission suffix. It converts deleteListener to a pointer and drops the count field, breaking compatibility so the suite fails, and its abstract test file depends on helpers in another test file.

A sound redesign with a shared state that keeps a master fd, which also fixes the newest-holder-closes-first case, but removing the count field and making deleteListener a pointer breaks every hidden test at compile time.

Matches the reference: it closes the leaked dup in reuse, gets the name from Addr() instead of File(), serializes Close under unixSocketsMu, makes double close safe and skips unlinking abstract sockets, with thorough tests covering both unix and unixgram.

Matches the reference: it closes the leaked dup'd fds, takes the name from Addr(), serializes Close under unixSocketsMu, adds a closed CAS returning net.ErrClosed and skips unlink for abstract sockets, with thorough tests covering every review requirement.

The code is essentially identical to the reference and fixes the leaked File() dups, double-close, the race and abstract-socket handling; its tests are solid, though the reuse test doesn't check that the surviving listener still accepts.
Code is byte-identical to the reference fix, with a solid test set; one reuse test does not check that the surviving holder still accepts connections.

A kept-open 'keeper' duplicate plus a shared count avoids fd leaks, unlinks on the last close under the lock, handles abstract sockets and double close, and makes newest-closes-first safe; it restructures more than needed but stays compatible with the existing internals.

A correct alternative that keeps a dup'd keeper listener in the map so later reuse never depends on a closed holder; it preserves the internal API, so hidden tests pass, but it is more invasive than the reference.

A heavy restructure adds a second mutex, changes listenerPool counting for reused sockets (a behavioral change to shutdown-delay logic), and also edits listeners.go. The abstract check ignores GOOS, and the internal API changes break the suite.
Adds a second mutex, wraps reused sockets in deleteListener and counts them in listenerPool (a semantic change), and edits listeners.go; this is far beyond the needed fix and fails all hidden tests.

A shared unixSocket state holds its own dup'd fd and a ref count, and Close is now idempotent, so the fix works and also covers the newest-holder-closes-first case. However, it changes deleteListener to a pointer type and removes unixListener.count, so the package suite fails, and the File() error path doesn't undo the listenerPool entry.
Refcounted shared-state design is race-safe, but it leaks a listenerPool reference when File() fails and its internal restructuring fails all hidden tests.
